readerTitle: Why neighbors Germany and Austria got opposite answers on organ donation
caseNote: 실제 정책 사례와 연구 (Johnson & Goldstein 2003, 유럽 국가들의 장기 기증 제도, 네덜란드 정책 변화). 사례 종류 규칙에 따라 real_company를 포함했습니다. 가상 적용 사례는 사내 팀(반복 회의)과 B2B 서비스(IT 관리 서비스)입니다.
insight: 기본값은 '결정하지 않는 사람'에 대한 결정이다. 사람들의 마음을 바꾸기보다 '응답하지 않으면 어떻게 되는가'를 설계하는 편이 결과를 더 크게 바꾼다.
misconception: 사람들이 행동하지 않는 건 정보나 설득이 부족해서다. 그러니 캠페인과 안내를 늘리면 해결된다.

sources.text: Johnson, E. J., & Goldstein, D. (2003). Do Defaults Save Lives? Science, 302(5649), 1338–1339. (국가별 동의율, 온라인 실험 42%/82%/79%)
Abadie, A., & Gay, S. (2006). The impact of presumed consent legislation on cadaveric organ donation: A cross-country study. Journal of Health Economics, 25(4), 599–620.
네덜란드 정부, 새 기증자법(Donorwet) 시행 안내 (2020년 옵트아웃 전환)
스페인 국립장기이식기구(ONT), 이식 코디네이터 중심의 '스페인 모델' 자료

factChecks.note: 차트 수치는 Johnson & Goldstein(2003)의 '유효 동의율'입니다. 덴마크 4.25%, 독일 12%, 영국 17.17%, 네덜란드 27.5%, 스웨덴 85.9%, 벨기에 98%, 프랑스 99.91%, 오스트리아 99.98%. 차트에서는 덴마크를 4.3, 영국을 17.2, 프랑스를 99.9로 반올림했습니다. 게시 전에 원문 그림과 대조하세요.
온라인 실험 수치는 같은 논문에 나옵니다. 옵트인 42%, 옵트아웃 82%, 강제 선택(중립) 79%. 참가자 수(161명)는 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.
네덜란드의 1998년 등록부 도입과 대규모 우편 캠페인은 Johnson & Goldstein 논문에 언급됩니다. 발송 규모(약 1,200만 통)가 확실하지 않아 카드에는 'millions of households'로만 적었습니다. 2020년 옵트아웃 전환 시점은 네덜란드 정부 자료로 확인하세요.
실제 기증률 차이는 등록 동의율 차이보다 작습니다. Abadie & Gay(2006)는 추정 동의 국가의 기증률이 다른 조건을 통제해도 대략 25~30% 높다고 보고합니다. 카드에는 'smaller but real'로만 적었습니다. 스페인의 높은 기증률을 제도 운영(이식 코디네이터)의 성과로 보는 해석은 ONT 자료와 관련 문헌으로 확인하세요.
독일과 오스트리아의 문화적 유사성은 원 논문이 제시한 비교 틀입니다. 두 나라의 제도는 이후 바뀌었을 수 있으므로 카드에서는 '2003년 연구 당시' 기준임을 밝혔습니다.

cards.title: Why neighbors Germany and Austria got opposite answers on organ donation
body: Germany and Austria share a language, a border and much of their culture. Yet in a 2003 study, about **12%** of Germans had consented to be organ donors. In Austria, the figure was nearly **100%**.
The difference wasn't in people's hearts. It was in how a form treated people who never filled it in.

image.label: Two nearly identical forms with one box checked differently
image.brief: 나란히 놓인 거의 똑같은 서류 두 장. 왼쪽은 체크박스가 비어 있고 오른쪽은 미리 체크되어 있음. 서류 위에 작은 하트 아이콘. 국기, 정부 문장, 실제 기관 로고는 쓰지 않음. 따뜻하고 차분한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Most people say yes. Few sign up.
body: You run a country's organ donor registry. Polls show most people support donation, but only a small share have registered. Patients are waiting.
What would move the numbers most?

options.text: Launch a big campaign and mail a sign-up form to every household
options.feedback: Campaigns raise awareness, but they still ask each person to act. Most good intentions stop right there.

options.text: Change what happens when someone gives no answer
options.feedback: This targets the biggest group: people who never decide. It works without changing anyone's mind, though it raises fair questions about consent.

options.text: Offer a cash reward for registering
options.feedback: Money may lift sign-ups, but it can make a gift feel like a sale and crowd out the reasons people give.

cards.title: Same question, different default.
body: In **opt-in** countries, you are a donor only if you sign up. In **opt-out** countries, you are a donor unless you say no. Effective consent rates in the 2003 study:
cards.callout: The Netherlands had mailed forms to millions of households. It still sat near the bottom.

image.label: Opt-in vs opt-out organ donation rates
image.brief: Two columns of countries: opt-in low teens vs opt-out near 100%.

cards.title: The default decides for people who don't decide.
body: A **default** is what happens when someone takes no action. On any form, a large group never answers, so the default quietly decides for them.
Defaults win for three reasons. Acting takes effort, even a little. The default looks like the recommended choice. And it sets the starting point, so changing it feels like giving something up.

image.label: A crowd walking along a default path, a few stepping off
image.brief: 넓은 길 위를 많은 사람이 그대로 걸어가고, 옆의 작은 갈림길로 몇 명만 빠지는 장면. 큰 길에 'No answer'라는 표지판. 단순한 플랫 인포그래픽 스타일.

cards.title: Asking everyone works almost as well.
body: The same researchers ran an online test. Asked to opt in, **42%** agreed to be donors. With an opt-out, **82%** stayed donors.
A third group had no default at all. They had to pick yes or no to continue, and **79%** said yes.
That's the less famous finding. You don't have to choose for people. Removing the option of *not answering* gets close to the same result, and everyone has made a real choice.

cards.title: A team inside a company
body: A company's operations team sees calendars full of recurring meetings nobody remembers starting. Asking managers to clean them up changes little.
So the team flips the default: recurring meetings now end after three months unless the organizer renews them with one click. Useful meetings get renewed. Forgotten ones simply end.
cards.softwareNote: In a software product, defaults are everywhere: notification settings, auto-renewal, privacy options. Most users never open settings, so whatever ships switched on becomes what most users get.

cards.title: A checked box is not an organ.
body: Registration isn't donation. Families, doctors and hospital systems decide what actually happens. Studies of real donation rates find the gap between opt-out and opt-in countries is smaller than the consent numbers, though still real.
Spain has among the highest donation rates, often credited to trained transplant coordinators in hospitals, not just its law.
And defaults chosen for people need public trust. Some countries debated opt-out for years before switching. The Netherlands moved to it in 2020.

cards.title: Now it's an IT services firm.
body: You manage IT for 60 small business clients. Every client should test restoring their backups each quarter. Few ever book the test, and one bad restore could sink a client.

options.text: Send clients a clear email explaining the risk and asking them to book
options.feedback: Honest and easy to do, but it still needs each client to act. Expect a few bookings, like the mailed forms.

options.text: Put a test on every client's calendar, with one-click reschedule or opt-out
options.feedback: Doing nothing now leads to a test, and clients keep full control. You trade a bit of scheduling work for far more tests.

options.text: Run the test automatically and add it to invoices without asking
options.feedback: Coverage goes up, but surprise charges damage trust. A good default is easy to see and easy to leave.

cards.title: Design the answer for people who never answer.
body: Before trying to persuade people, decide what happens when they do nothing. Make that outcome good for them, visible and easy to change, or ask everyone to choose.
**Try it today:** pick one form, contract or setting your customers or team see. Write down what happens if someone ignores it. Is that the outcome you want?
